openalex_display_name: Unhoming the Pigeon: Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Pigeons’ storied history and waning fortunes have drawn the attention of many writers, including Ahmed Ali. Ali’s 1940 novel Twilight in Delhi uses pigeon imagery to link together the spatial trope of homelessness and the temporal trope of slouching toward extinction. The novel is about the long decline of a Muslim family under British imperial rule. Its patriarch often meditates on the tragedy of cultural extinction, and his pigeon loft is made a synecdoche for that threatened culture. Early critics frequently read Twilight as a nostalgic lament for the Mughal Empire that preceded British occupation in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. However, as more recent scholarship has argued, Ali likely intended for his novel to be, not a call to restore the lost precolonial past, but a way of using residual elements of that past to galvanize a postcolonial future. This chapter argues that Twilight in Delhi, like other twentieth-century texts, makes pigeons emblems of homelessness and extinction, but it also refigures the birds as a sign for survival, futurity, and change. In Ali’s vision, those who are in the wrong place or the wrong era are also those who point to other possibilities for social and political life, beyond the cultural and biological depredations of British occupation. This was a powerful anticolonial message in the 1940s. It can be powerful again today, in the era of climate change and the sixth extinction, as an insistent call to make the victims of imperial capitalism—including displaced people and displaced animals—the center of the just community that, one hopes, will succeed us.

openalex_display_name: The Invasion
openalex_abstract: The Invasion, a novel originally published in 1932, marked the debut of historical novelist Janet Lewis, who went on to write numerous poems and short stories as well as the novels The Wife of Martin Guerre and The Trial of Soren Quist. Lewis grew up in the Lake country of the Old Northwest and The Invasion is based on family stories she heard as a child.The Invasion displays well-researched historical accuracy, an innate understanding of and feeling for Native American culture enhanced by the author's fluency in the Ojibway language, and an economy of style that is remarkable for a first novel. In 1790, John Johnston, a cultivated young Irishman, came to the far corner of the Northwest Territory to make his fortune intending to spend only a year. Instead he married Ozhah-guscoday- wayquay (The Woman of the Glade), daughter of the Ojibway chief Waub- ojeeg, and settled on the St. Mary's River. Together they founded a family that was loved, respected, and famous throughout the region for honesty, fairness, and hospitality. Their home was the center of culture for the area and for every visiting traveler, Native American or white. The Invasion chronicles a time when one culture violently supplanted another even as it depicts a family that blends two cultures together. Henry Rowe Schoolcraft considered the Johnston family his most valued connection to the Native American population. He eventually married Jane Johnston, daughter of John and The Woman of the Glade, and remain close to her entire family. In his diary, Schoolcraft wrote of the Johnstons, "I have in fact stumbled, as it were, on the only family in Northwest America who could in Indian lore have acted as my guide, philosopher, and friend."

openalex_display_name: COMPARING INDIAN AND WESTERN RESPONSES TO PANDEMICS: EXISTENTIAL CRISES IN REBATI, A LIFE MISSPENT, AND TWILIGHT IN DELHI
openalex_abstract: This paper explores the existential themes in Indian and Western pandemic narratives, focusing on how pandemics are depicted in literature and their impact on human experience. Through a comparative analysis of works such as Rebati by Fakir Mohan Senapati, A Life Misspent by Suryakant Tripathi Nirala, and Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali, alongside Western texts like The Plague by Albert Camus, The Last Man by Mary Shelley, and Love in the Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez, this study examines how pandemics serve as catalysts for existential crises and reflections on mortality, love, and human connection. In Indian narratives, pandemics often highlight social decay, personal suffering, and the impact of colonialism, while Western narratives engage more directly with existentialism, absurdism, and resistance. In García Márquez's novel, love becomes an existential response to death, providing meaning amidst suffering. By contrasting these narratives, this paper demonstrates that while pandemics bring death and despair, they also offer profound reflections on life’s meaning. The study shows how different cultural contexts shape literary responses to disease, illustrating both shared human concerns and distinctive cultural interpretations of suffering, mortality, and the quest for meaning. Ultimately, this comparative study offers new insights into the role of pandemics in shaping existential thought.

Susanna Ashton raises a number of intriguing questions at the beginning of her innovative analysis of literary collaboration in Gilded Age America. Calling attention to the surprisingly large number of literary works that were written by more than one hand during this period, Ashton wants us to rethink what it means to be an author, particularly when that concept is, essentially, divorced from its conventional association with an individuated creative consciousness. Why was this period so conducive to collaboration? she asks. “By examining the ways in which collaborative fictions were assembled and conceived,” Ashton argues, “we can see how the profession of authorship was variously defined and how those definitions were constructed in terms of one another” (p. 2). Ashton pursues this topic by analyzing— and, in some instances, resurrecting—a range of collaborative fictions from the period. She begins with possibly the first instance of a co-written novel, The Gilded Age (1873) by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, and proceeds chronologically with assessments of The King's Men (1884, jointly authored by Robert Grant, John T. Wheelwright, John Boyle O'Reilly, and Frederic Jesup Stimson), the various literary collaborations of Brander T. Matthews, and The Whole Family (1908), probably the most familiar group novel of the period, which featured twelve writers whose work was associated with the Harper publishing empire.

John Bennett (1865–1956) was born in Chil-licothe, Ohio, and as a young man in the Midwest worked chiefly as a journalist and writer of adventure tales for youths. In his thirties, he enrolled in the Art Students' League in New York, and while there he published a perennially popular children's tale, Master Skylark (1897), set in Shakespearean England. Soon thereafter he married into the South Carolina gentry—his wife was a granddaughter of the antebellum writer Louisa McCord—and became active in the cultural life of Charleston. In the 1920s and 1930s, he was the central figure in the flickering literary activity in the Carolina low country that Harlan Greene and others call the Charleston renaissance. In Mr. Skylark, Greene relates the story of those things. He does so commendably, despite the problems in his enterprise. Literarily, Bennett's oeuvre is marginal at best, as is most of the work of his Charleston and low-country contemporaries, though the best-known item in that work, DuBose Heyward's Porgy (1925), remains well known and appealing because of its rendering in George Gershwin's Porg y and Bess (1935). Greene has dealt with the literary marginality of Bennett's works by summary rather than critique and with the Charleston renaissance by focusing on Bennett's relations with such luminaries as Hey-ward and Hervey Allen and his activities in the Poetry Society of South Carolina. In addition, Greene has written Bennett's biography largely in Bennett's own words, taken from the voluminous Bennett papers at the South Carolina Historical Society. While this has its usefulness, it gives Greene's account much the character of autobiography, with an attendant lack of critique.

The Missing Mahatma: Ahmed Ali and the Aesthetics of Muslim Anticolonialism
openalex_abstract: Nationalist Politics and Delhi By 1940, when Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi was published, it would have been increasingly difficult, though not impossible, to be a Muslim and a nationalist in the united Provinces. a few important figures had managed to navigate the problem of communal loyalties: Shibli Numani, Abul Kalam Azad and the Ali brothers had all publicly defended and made alliances with the Indian national Congress (Lelyveld 2004). In 1941, Jamaat-e-Ulema-e-Hind (later Jamaat-e-Islami), a relatively powerful collective of Muslim ulama from North India, would also come out in defense of an undivided India in opposition to Jinnah and the Muslim League and their “two nation theory” (Sarkar 1989). Furthermore, the Congress paid lip service to the idea of speaking for all of India by raising the slogan that Muslims were welcome under its large tent Jalal 2001). Still, the contradiction between a Muslim identity and a nationalist one would have been palpable. Muslims appeared to give up longstanding internal debates and fall into rank behind the Muslim League by the 1942 elections, while the Muslims in the Congress were more and more seen as Muslims in name only, and were thoroughly critiqued for their heterodoxies. Leading Muslims in the Congress were devout, but the larger chunk of the Muslim membership would have been composed of secular, Western-educated, professional and left-leaning individuals. The Communist Party, when it entered into the Congress, brought with it thousands of young, secularized Muslims who were hostile to religiosity and saw only the trappings of orthodoxy in it.

openalex_abstract: Another Part of the ForestThomas H. McKee and the Suppression of Sister Carrie Donald Pizer (bio) Although a great deal has been written about the alleged suppression of Theodore Dreiser’s Sister Carrie by Doubleday, Page and Co. during the summer of 1900, almost all of these accounts derive from Dreiser’s own version of the event and are thus deeply colored by his never-ending anger at the injustice done him, his novel, and American literary culture in general. The principal participants in the event were Dreiser, Arthur Henry (a minor novelist and a close friend at the time), Frank Norris (the novelist, who worked part-time as a reader for Doubleday, Page and who had read the manuscript for the firm), Frank N. Doubleday (the senior partner) and his wife, Neltje Blanchan De Graff Doubleday (a prolific and successful nature writer), Walter Hines Page (a former newspaperman and magazine editor and the junior partner), Henry Lanier (son of the poet Sidney Lanier and an editor at the firm), and Thomas H. McKee (the firm’s lawyer).1 Henry and Norris strongly supported publication of the novel throughout the controversy. Page and Lanier initially endorsed publication but later reversed their position. And Doubleday and his wife adamantly opposed publication of the novel once they read it. Norris died in 1902 without having written on the matter, and Henry, Page, Lanier, and the Doubledays also failed to record their versions in any fulness.2 Dreiser, however, devoted much time and energy for the remainder of his long career to promulgating his own account, beginning with a lively interview with a St. Louis newspaper in 1902 (“Author”). Besides taking it up again and again in interviews, he repeated it in letters to friends and in autobiographical articles.3 The furor over the suppression of The “Genius” in 1916 reinforced his resentment of the earlier suppression. In later years the story received its fullest and most resonant recounting in H. L. Mencken’s essay on Dreiser in his 1917 A Book of Prefaces (67–148) and in [End Page 60] Dorothy Dudley’s lengthy presentation of it in her 1932 Forgotten Frontiers: Dreiser and the Land of the Free (166–70, 180–84). The suppression narrative, as constructed by Dreiser and repeated by his supporters, consisted of three main elements: The novel’s initial warm welcome by Norris and Page; then the firm’s efforts to withdraw its acceptance, based on Mrs. Doubleday’s belief that the work was immoral; and finally the firm’s decision to proceed with publication because of Dreiser’s insistence that it honor its acceptance, but to do so without promoting the book in any way except for sending out review copies. On 23 January 1949, shortly after the publication of Robert H. Elias’s Theodore Dreiser: Apostle of Nature, Thomas H. McKee, the sole surviving participant in the events of the summer of 1900, wrote Elias from California, where he had been living for some forty years, to inquire whether Elias cared to receive his recollections of some of the events depicted in the biography. It is clear from this timing that Elias did not know when preparing his biography that McKee was alive and had therefore not contacted him in connection with it. Over the next seven years McKee wrote Elias four additional letters, the most important of which, and by far the lengthiest, is his fourteen-page typescript letter of 23 March 1949, transcribed below. Elias drew upon McKee’s letters for a footnote in his 1959 Letters of Theodore Dreiser (2: 420) and for the revision of one sentence and the addition of a second in the 1970 Emended Edition of his biography.4 After his retirement from Cornell, he donated his Dreiser collection, including the McKee letters, to the Cornell University Library, where they now reside. Later biographers have been equally spare in their use of the letters. W. A. openalex_display_name: Paternalistic Authority in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi: a Stylistic Analysis
openalex_abstract: The linguistic study of Pakistani literary texts has become a rich ground for researchers in both Applied Linguistics and Literary Studies. This study applies transitivity in analyzing the linguistic patterns in which paternal figure’s authority is stylistically foregrounded, adding to the text’s subversive force in Ali’s Twilight in Delhi (2007). The analysis will reveal how paternal elements have a particular impact on the characters’ discursive subjectivity. This stylistic strategy foregrounds the paternalistic authority in the novel. This study explored the dominant male figure in a family; represented by a father in the novel delineates his son’s opportunities which open up new perspectives on paternal authority in the social and affective relationship concerning the son’s efforts at self-determination by the paternalistic authority that is often at odds with his son’s aspirations and sense of self. The tension that underlies the entire novel pivots around the efforts of a young man in Delhi to achieve a measure of self-determination in the context of rigid paternalistic authority, which is embodied in the narrative. The study has implications for explorations on the interface between language and literature and further research.

openalex_display_name: Representation of Implicit Domestic Culture in Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Exploring implicit domestic culture in Twilight in Delhi (2007)by Ahmed Ali, the study applies theoretical framework of M.A.K Halliday’s Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG) which asserts that meanings lies in the clause. The main argument of the paper is to linguistically examine the effects of social imbalance within family structure. It also argues that language is not neutral for it carries ideology in it; therefore, hegemonic power relations and its manipulation are explored leading to its effects on different lives.Data are analyzed qualitatively at clause level, using tools of ideational, interpersonal and textual meta-functions of language.As a guide, 19 Tables are formed to show and compares the processes according to the main issue of the study. Linguistic analysis of the text is done by using Transitivity, Mood, Rheme and Theme to identify power relations in Eastern families. The paper examined different sorts of 19 situations where the norms of implicit family culture were noticed. The study also discovered that the male members of the family exercised power over the female characters. The study is going to be an addition to future researchers of CDA to use SFG to literature to highlight and analyze social imbalance.

openalex_display_name: In the Twilight of Nostalgia
openalex_abstract: The article maps out the affinities between Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi (1940) and Naguib Mahfouz’s Palace Walk (1956). It traces the central mood of nostalgia for a lost past in the two novels and demonstrates how this ambivalent mood plays out in three respects: in the characters’ leisure activities, marked by their indolence and retrospective yearning; in the exaggerated assertion of patriarchal self-importance, compensating for a loss of actual political significance; and in the fraught relationship with the British. These three issues coalesce in the male protagonists’ amorous exploits, which link with the production of traditional poetry and song, serial adultery and the cultural clash between British and vernacular culture. In the final section, I discuss the two novels from the perspective of literary history and propose that they may be typical of a genre of the Muslim novel on its emergence from colonialism.

openalex_display_name: Staging Realism and the Ambivalence of Nationalism in the Colonial Novel
openalex_abstract: This essay moves away from accounts of social realism, which privilege its political aims over its aesthetic innovations. I argue that social realism written under colonialism was part of a larger intellectual project to rethink the desirability and content of nationalism by testing the limitations and plasticity of the realist mode. I look specifically at moments of self-referentiality in social realist writing as well as in the repeated claims by writers themselves about the mimetic purpose of social realism. In this way, I show how literary realism in the colony lived the dual life of representing the material world and taking on a materiality of its own, as language marked by aspiration and potentiality. This “projective realism” is epitomized by Ahmed Ali's 1940 novel Twilight in Delhi. Twilight, by offering an interpretation of history as a performance, a series of snapshots, and gestures definable in synchronic time, provides an idiom from which to rethink the conventional discourse upon which nationalism is founded and raises a profound ambivalence as to which nation this “nationalist” novel in fact references.

openalex_display_name: Languishing in Ahmed Ali’s Delhi
openalex_abstract: Ahmed Ali, a founding member of the All-India Progressive Writers Association (PWA), was castigated for his first novel in English which failed, according to its critics, to address the pressing needs of India’s poor and suffering. Ali’s Twilight in Delhi is surprisingly committed to passivity, given the writer’s pioneering affiliation with the activist group. Instead of representing activist struggle, his novel depicts the death of a culture and its lingering afterlife, ironically via the English language and literary form. While there is no doubting the novel’s opposition to empire, it embraces passivity as a formal challenge to the ideological demands of the PWA, whose members openly derided it. Two fragile cultural forms linger even after their extinction in the novel: Urdu poetry, especially the ghazal form, and the ancient art of pigeon-keeping. In the end, the novel aligns itself with the vanquished and vulnerable – whether art or animal – and submits to an imperial form that will paradoxically ensure their survival.
